newsitem.title: UK: "Morning-after" drivers may just be hung over.
newsitem.headline: "Morning-after" drivers may just be hung over.

text.p: You've had a few too many drinks at a dinner party, your head is pounding and you fear you are still too drunk to drive to work.
Not necessarily, British researchers have found. They said among men, anyway, the body gets rid of most of the alcohol after a night's sleep.
Neil Wright and colleagues at the University of Leicester tested 58 men, keeping track of how much they drank in an evening and then testing their alcohol levels in the morning.
"Partners and friends helped verify quantities and the time that drinking stopped. All men ate either shortly before or during drinking," he wrote in a letter to the Lancet medical journal.
They then tested the men -- 44 of whom said they had hangovers -- for alcohol with a breathalyser.
"Nobody exceeded the U.K. drink drive limit on morning testing," he wrote. "Thirty men recorded zero breath alcohol concentrations, five of whom consumed more than 20 units."

He said his study indicated that social drinkers, who usually eat as they drink and who do not drink all night, are probably all right to drive the next day, despite clinical tests indicating otherwise.
Those tests did not reflect real conditions, he said. Volunteers usually had to fast during the tests, and took the alcohol all at once.

"Alcohol metabolism during prolonged drinking produces lower post-drinking concentrations than after single-dose intake," he said. "Food decreases alcohol concentrations through its effect on alcohol absorption."
One unit of alcohol equals a half-pint (225 ml) of beer, a glass of wine or a small serving of spirits.
The liver metabolises one unit of alcohol, roughly equivalent to a small glass of wine, per hour. But most doctors advise not driving at all for at least 12 hours after having a drink.
